newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO and east Europe hail Clinton triumph.
newsitem.headline: NATO and east Europe hail Clinton triumph.

text.p: NATO, facing tough choices over the future of its Bosnia peace force and its planned eastwards expansion in Europe, on Wednesday welcomed U.S. President Bill Clinton's re-election, but reacted warily to the new Congress.
"The victory represents continuity, but Congress is playing an increasing role in foreign policy and we will have to look closely at that," one senior alliance official said.
He said several old senators known to attach great importance to the transatlantic link embodied by the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation had disappeared from the scene.

"Men like Sam Nunn (veteran chairman of the Armed Forces committee) who retired at this election who were pro-NATO, we have to hope their successors are equally pro-NATO, internationalist-minded," he added.

NATO officials stressed both Clinton and his Republican opponent Bob Dole were in favour of the alliance's planned expansion eastwards to take in new members from former communist Europe, but said a hostile Congress could delay ratification.
That view was eched by eastern and central European states clamouring to slip under the West's security cloak as an insurance policy against a newly expansionist Russia.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic lead the race to get in, but a host of other countries, including the key strategic Baltic states, are hot on their heels.
While wooing voters of Central European origin during the campaign, Clinton spoke for NATO's enlargement by 1999, while Dole promised a date of 1998.

Analysts said the key question was how many supporters of enlargement had been elected to the Senate, which will have to approve the necessary changes to NATO's founding Washington Treaty with a two-thirds majority -- 67 out of the 100 votes.

"We have been observing these elections fairly calmly for some time, as both candidates spoke clearly for enlarging NATO by 1999 -- Dole even gave an earlier date," senior opposition parliamentarian Janusz Onyszkiewicz told Reuters.
"What is relevant to us is the election to the Senate -- that those who back enlargement should keep their position," said Onyszkiewicz of the Union for Freedom (UW) party.
He said such views were not held along party lines in the Senate and it would take a while before Poland knew if ratification had enough support there.
"We will not know for some time. This depends on how long the new administration will take to win over the Senate."

Onyszkiewicz, respected across party lines as a top authority on NATO, said Warsaw's negotiators had been dealing with Clinton's entourage for some time and would find it easier to continue than to start with a different team.
Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski sent a letter of congratulations and best wishes to Clinton.
"As a result of your second election victory your mission has taken on a new historic dimension. All in Poland highly value your consistent involvement in the process of enlarging NATO," he wrote.

Romanian President Ion Iliescu said he hoped Clinton would back his country's bid to join the alliance and the European Union. Romania is not expected to be invited to open membership talks at a special NATO summit next year.

"I hope the Clinton administration will support Romania in all its efforts at integration into European and Atlantic institutions. I don't think there will be any change in the policy of the Clinton administration towards Romanian whatever forces make up the government."
Slovenian Foreign Minister Davorin Kracun whose country has recently emerged as the most likely outsider to win swift admission said Slovenia would receive strong U.S. support.

"The outcome of U.S. presidential election is very good for Slovenia as relations with the U.S. have improved significantly since a period of sceptical relations in 1991 and 1992," Kracun told a news conference.
